newsitem.title: BELGIUM: New Belgian body find reopens protection charges.
newsitem.headline: New Belgian body find reopens protection charges.

text.p: Belgium, still reeling from the discovery last August of the bodies of four young girls and evidence of bungled police investigations, was plunged into new shock on Thursday with the discovery of another dead girl.
The discovery added fuel to charges of police and judicial ineptitude or corruption.
The decomposed body of Loubna Benaissa, nine years old when she disappeared on a local shopping trip in August 1992, was discovered in a steel trunk under a garage in central Brussels.

To make matters worse, the girl's body was found just round the corner from where she lived in Brussels' Ixelles suburb in a street that police had searched extensively shortly after her disappearance.
A man who worked at the garage has been arrested. Police had questioned him shortly after Loubna disappeared but released him.
Denis Lejeune, the father of eight-year-old Julie whose body was found last August buried in a house owned by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, voiced the general discontent.
"It is unbelievable. Once again the investigators had all the information from the outset. And it took so many years...," Lejeune told Belga newsagency.
"It is exactly the same as our case. Now no one can doubt that there has been protection," he said.

Even Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck expressed bewilderment at the Brussels investigations. "Working on the same information Neufchateau found something and Brussels nothing," he told a news conference.
"There is once again this feeling that something was not quite right in the inquiry," he said.

The cases of all missing Belgian children have, since the summer, been centralised under public prosecutor Michel Bourlet and a team of investigating magistrates based in the southern city of Neufchateau.

Laurent Arnauts, the Benaissa family lawyer, told RTBF television the fact that the family was Moroccan might have been a factor influencing the inquiry but it should not obscure the fact that there were obviously deep flaws in the investigation.
By coincidence, a parliamentary commission investigating the original bungled police investigations in the search for Dutroux's four victims, ended its public hearings on Wednesday.

The commission has been sitting for five months during which it has taken testimony under oath -- sometimes televised, sometimes behind closed doors -- from parents, policemen, gendarmes, judges and prosecutors.

Clear contradictions have repeatedly come to light about who told what to whom and when. And increasingly the commission has begun focusing on the possibilities that for unknown reasons Dutroux benefited from official protection.
The revelations have repeatedly shocked the Belgian public as they stayed glued to their television screens.
The commission will spend the first three days of next week combing its findings for preliminary conclusions and is supposed to produce a report on March 15.
But president Marc Verwilghen said the members had decided to ask the leaders of the parliamentary factions on Thursday next week for an extension to April 15 to pursue the protection investigations.
